report:
## Conclusion

The claim that "capsaicin treats breast cancer in humans" is **not supported by current evidence**. Capsaicin has shown antiproliferative, pro-apoptotic, and cell-cycle-arresting effects on breast cancer cell lines (e.g., MCF-7, MDA-MB-231, BT-20) in laboratory studies, and it modulates pathways like EGFR/HER-2 signaling in vitro (nature.com/articles/onc2009335). However, these findings come exclusively from cell-culture and animal (xenograft) models, not human patients with breast cancer.

Reviews of the field explicitly note that despite decades of preclinical interest, "the anticancer efficacy is currently limited" in humans, and poor oral bioavailability plus dose-limiting side effects (burning sensation, GI pain, nausea) hamper its development as an actual cancer therapeutic (frontiersin.org/journals/oncology/articles/10.3389/fonc.2022.908487/full; pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10177684/). A comprehensive 2024 review likewise describes capsaicin's oncologic role as still largely preclinical, calling for further trials (thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/pdf/10.1055/a-2309-5581.pdf).

The only well-established human clinical use of capsaicin in breast cancer patients is **symptomatic**, not curative: topical high-concentration capsaicin patches are used to relieve chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy and post-surgical neuropathic pain after breast cancer treatment (CAPTRANE and QUCIP trials), not to treat the tumor itself (mdpi.com/2072-6694/18/14/2355; pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11763653/).

Additionally, epidemiological data on chili/capsaicin intake and cancer risk are mixed and inconsistent, with some studies even suggesting increased cancer risk with high chili consumption, further undermining any protective/therapeutic narrative.

**Bottom line:** Capsaicin shows anticancer activity against breast cancer cells in lab settings, but there is no clinical trial evidence that it treats breast cancer in humans. It is currently approved only for pain management in cancer patients, not as an anticancer agent.
